quote: Aufgabe: Einen Garten in 3 [-gleiche-] inhaltsgleiche Teile so zuteilen, dass die Gesammtlänge der verwandten Zäune ein Minimum wird.
english: Problem: to divide a garden into 3 parts of equal area in such a way that the total length of the fences used becomes a minimum.
topic: A garden-division minimum problem, quotations from Kronecker's lectures on definite integrals (Darwinian analogy, functions of one variable as limit cases, Fourier double integral, passage to Poisson's integral via Abel's theorem, a convergence theorem for Fourier series), and the Codazzi formulas applied to Hilbert's theorem on surfaces of constant negative curvature.

triage.modern_statement: Isoperimetric partition problem: given a planar region Ω (the 'garden'), find a partition of Ω into three regions of equal area, each |Ω|/3, that minimizes the total length of the interior boundaries (the fences). In modern terms this is a constrained minimal-perimeter (soap-film or 'cluster in a container') partition problem. Minimizers consist of circular arcs or straight segments meeting in threes at 120° and meeting ∂Ω orthogonally. The note does not specify the shape of the garden, and it is unclear whether the outer boundary fence is counted. If the outer boundary is counted and the shape is free, the problem becomes the planar triple bubble problem.
triage.answered_by: This is solved for the natural special cases, but I found no general solution for an arbitrary garden shape. For a disk-shaped garden with given areas (equal areas included), A. Cañete and M. Ritoré proved that the standard three-arc 120° graph is the unique minimizer (arXiv math/0307207, Indiana Univ. Math. J., 2004). For the free-shape version, where the outer fence is counted, W. Wichiramala proved the planar triple bubble conjecture (J. reine angew. Math. 567 (2004), DOI 10.1515/CRLL.2004.011).

evidence.claim: Cañete and Ritoré prove that the unique least-perimeter partition of the unit disk into three regions of prescribed areas is the standard graph.
Wichiramala proved the planar triple bubble conjecture: the standard triple bubble is the unique least-perimeter way to enclose and separate three regions of given areas.
Wichiramala's proof was published in Crelle's journal (DOI 10.1515/CRLL.2004.011).
Least-perimeter partitions of the disk into N regions are still being studied, which shows the topic is an ongoing research line.
Minimal-length partitions of domains with equal-area constraints are studied in recent work.

triage.why: The note is a clear minimal-partition (isoperimetric cluster) problem. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th. The cases that can be stated precisely were solved in 2004: the disk by Cañete and Ritoré, and the free planar triple bubble by Wichiramala. Confidence is medium for two reasons. First, Hilbert does not give the garden's shape, so 'solved' only applies to these standard cases; for a general region the answer depends on the shape, and I found no general solution. Second, my search budget ran out before I could check other shapes such as squares or general convex gardens. The 2018–2021 papers show that partition problems with area constraints are still actively researched. I found no source linking Hilbert's diary entry to this later work.
